transcript.content: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um... well, I guess I'm here because I just... I really can't shake this feeling. It's this incredibly heavy, just completely hopeless feeling that's been dragging me down. I'm a civil engineer, so I spend all day thinking about structures and loads and stability, and... well, it honestly feels like everything I built after my divorce has just completely collapsed. I spent so much time and energy after the marriage ended trying to lay down a new foundation, you know? Getting my life back on track, making sure everything was solid and secure and done right. I really thought I had it all stabilized. 

But now it's like... it's like the supports just gave out out of nowhere. And I'm just sitting under it. I'm just sitting under all the rubble and the weight of it, and I can't move. I wake up and that heavy feeling is just sitting right on top of me, and I try to figure out how to fix it, how to clear the debris, but I just feel so entirely hopeless about all of it. I just sit there under the weight of everything I tried to build.
Have you ever felt this way for a period of two weeks or longer at any point in your life before this current experience?

Well, as for before... it's honestly hard to untangle everything in my head right now because time just feels so distorted when you're in the middle of it. But if you're asking about this current... this specific heavy feeling? It's been about two weeks of this. Exactly two weeks, actually, since the bottom just completely fell out on me. 

And the thing is, it wasn't just a slow decline, which is why it's so hard to process. It was this totally out-of-control shift. Because right before this, I was just so intensely wired. I mean, my brain was running at absolute maximum capacity, just vibrating with all this energy, and I thought I was managing every single thing in my life perfectly. I was just going and going. But then the shift happened, and I had absolutely no control over it. I went from being that intensely wired to just... crashing. A complete structural failure. And that crash, that feeling of being trapped under the weight of it all like I was saying... that's what's been going on for about two weeks now. Every single day for the last fourteen days, just dealing with the whiplash of that shift from being so up and wired to just hitting the concrete, and not being able to dig myself out.
During that period before you crashed, when you felt so intensely wired and energetic, how many days in a row did that state last?

How many days... I mean... I really, honestly don't have a specific number for you. It’s so frustrating to even try to think about it right now because my brain is just so heavy, but back then... when I was in that state, time just didn't function the way it usually does. 

It’s like... well, it’s like asking someone caught in a wind tunnel to count the debris flying past them. You’re just in it, you know? You’re just moving at this incredible velocity and the whole concept of a standard twenty-four-hour 'day' just completely loses its structural integrity. I was so intensely focused on everything, just drafting and redesigning and pushing all these ideas forward, that the boundaries between, say, Monday and Tuesday or Wednesday just totally dissolved. It felt like one long, continuous, high-voltage current. 

I remember thinking that my internal motor was finally operating at the exact right frequency, but because I was moving so incredibly fast, looking back now from under all this rubble and trying to put a pin in a calendar to say 'it was exactly this many days'... I just can't do it. The timeline is completely blurred together. So I really couldn't tell you how many days in a row it was. I just know it felt like it was going to last forever, right up until the exact second the supports snapped.

During that period when you were feeling so intensely wired and energetic, did you find that your behavior was so out of character or disruptive that others around you, like your friends, family, or colleagues, became concerned or insisted that you needed to slow down?

Well... yeah, people definitely noticed. I mean, you can't really hide it when the entire framework of how you operate just completely shifts. My supervisor at the engineering firm... he's usually this very hands-off guy, you know, trusts me completely with the structural analyses and the client presentations because I’ve always been so meticulous. But during that time, when I was just buzzing with all that electricity, I started making these really... well, questionable calls. I was approving material specs that I normally would have triple-checked, and I was just so impatient with everyone else's pace. 

I remember this one project meeting specifically—it was a Tuesday, I think, or maybe Thursday, it doesn't matter—but we were reviewing the load-bearing calculations for this commercial build, and I just completely fell apart in the middle of the conference room. Not crying, but just... my thoughts were moving so fast I couldn't articulate them, and I was snapping at the junior engineers because they couldn't see the vision I had. It was so disruptive that my supervisor actually pulled me aside afterward and told me he had to take me off all active project decisions. He said I was a liability, which... God, hearing that as an engineer, that you are the weak point in the structure, it just destroyed me. 

And it wasn't just at work, either. At home, everything just degraded. I completely stopped keeping up with my basic routines. I wasn't doing laundry, I wasn't eating properly, my apartment was just covered in blueprints and half-finished sketches that made sense to me at the time but probably looked like madness to anyone else. My sister came over because she hadn't heard from me, and she was terrified. She said I was talking a mile a minute and pacing, and then... well, then the crash started happening. The thoughts got so dark and so heavy so fast, and I was so overwhelmed by the sheer velocity of it all that I actually told her I didn't feel safe being alone in my own head. She ended up taking me straight to the emergency department because I just... I didn't feel safe with my own thoughts. So, yes, it was incredibly disruptive, and everyone around me could see the collapse happening before I even realized the supports were failing.
During that time when you were feeling so intensely wired, did you ever feel like you were seeing, hearing, or believing things that others around you were not experiencing or could not verify?

Seeing or hearing things? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my brain was moving at absolute warp speed, and the thoughts were bouncing off the walls of my skull like ricocheting bullets, but I wasn't... I wasn't hallucinating, if that's what you mean. I wasn't hearing voices or seeing things that weren't there. 

It was more just this intense, almost aggressive clarity about the things that *were* there. Like, I'd look at a blueprint and I'd swear I could see the stress fractures forming in the steel beams before they even poured the concrete. I felt like I had this hyper-awareness, this elevated understanding of structural integrity that nobody else in the firm could grasp. I remember trying to explain it to one of the senior partners—I had cornered him near the espresso machine, and I was just going on and on about how the entire grid system of the city was fundamentally flawed and how I was the only one who could redesign it to prevent a catastrophic collapse. I truly believed I was operating on this higher plane of engineering genius. 

But it wasn't a delusion in the sense that I thought I was, I don't know, a prophet or talking to aliens or anything. It was just this deeply inflated sense of my own capabilities. I just thought I was the smartest person in the room, the only one who could see the big picture. And the frustration of them not seeing it... it was maddening. I remember looking at their faces, just these blank, confused stares while I was practically vibrating with all these revolutionary ideas, and thinking, 'Why are you all moving so slowly? Why can't you see the math the way I see the math?' But no, I wasn't seeing visions or hearing things. It was all just my own thoughts, just amplified and accelerated to a point where they were completely unmanageable.
